title: Performance and accessibility pass
goal: Measure ApplyTrack with Lighthouse and axe, then fix what matters until both scores are strong.

concepts: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS
Lighthouse in DevTools: performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO
Bundle analysis: ng build --stats-json and a bundle analyser
Lazy-load heavy libraries (Chart.js only on the dashboard)
axe DevTools for accessibility issues; manual keyboard and screen reader checks
Caching static assets (hashed filenames + long cache headers in Nginx)

build.task: On the live ApplyTrack: run Lighthouse (mobile) on login, applications and dashboard, and axe on every page; record the starting scores in docs/quality.md. Fix: lazy-load Chart.js with @defer or a dynamic import, analyse the bundle and remove anything unnecessary, add long-lived cache headers for hashed assets in Nginx (and no-cache for index.html), reserve space for charts and images to avoid layout shift, and fix every axe issue (contrast, labels, landmarks, heading order). Test with keyboard only and with a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver or TalkBack) on one full journey. Record the after scores.
acceptance: Before and after Lighthouse scores recorded for 3 pages
Performance 90+ and Accessibility 95+ on mobile for all 3
Chart.js no longer in the initial bundle
Zero axe violations
Cache headers: hashed assets cached long, index.html not cached
One screen-reader journey completed and written up

hints: Nginx: location ~* \.(js|css|woff2|png|svg)$ { expires 1y; add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable"; } and location = /index.html { add_header Cache-Control "no-cache"; }

@defer (on viewport) { } @placeholder {
} keeps Chart.js out of the main bundle and reserves its space.
Run Lighthouse in an incognito window: extensions skew the results.
proof: Commit with fixes and docs/quality.md showing before and after.

explainBack.q: Why should hashed JS files be cached for a year but index.html not cached?
lookFor: hash changes when content changes so new files get new URLs
index.html points to the latest hashes
caching index.html would keep users on old versions

explainBack.q: Which fix improved your scores the most, and why?

lastHintExplanation: Build tools put a content hash in each file name, so a changed file gets a new URL, which makes it safe to cache old ones forever. index.html is the entry point that references the current hashes, so it must always be fetched fresh, or users would keep loading last week's app.

title: Polish: onboarding, empty states and one stretch feature
goal: Turn a working app into one that feels finished.

concepts: First-run experience: what a brand-new user sees
Helpful empty states with a clear next action
Microcopy: button labels, error messages, confirmations
Toasts with undo for destructive actions
Stretch features: CSV export, keyboard shortcuts, reminders

resources.title: Nielsen Norman Group: Error message guidelines

build.task: Polish ApplyTrack: a first-run welcome on the empty dashboard with 'Add your first application' and 'Load sample data' buttons (a server endpoint that seeds 10 sample applications for the current user); rewrite every error message to say what happened and what to do; add Undo to delete (soft delete or a delayed request); and build ONE stretch feature: CSV export of the filtered list (server endpoint with correct Content-Type and Content-Disposition, escaping commas and quotes), or keyboard shortcuts (n = new, / = search, ? = help dialog). Ship it with tests and a README update.
acceptance: New users see a helpful welcome, not a blank dashboard
'Load sample data' works and is scoped to the current user
Every error message says what happened and what to do next
Deleting can be undone for a few seconds
One stretch feature shipped with tests and documented

hints: CSV escaping: wrap a field in double quotes if it contains a comma, quote or newline, and double any quotes inside: '"' + value.replaceAll('"', '""') + '"'.

Download headers: res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/csv; charset=utf-8'); res.setHeader('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="applications.csv"'). Prefix the file with a BOM ('\uFEFF') so Excel reads ₹ and other non-ASCII characters correctly.
Undo pattern: remove from the UI immediately, show a toast with Undo for 5 seconds, and only call DELETE when the toast expires (or use a deleted_at column).
proof: Commit with polish changes and the stretch feature.

explainBack.q: Show a before-and-after error message and explain why the new one is better.
How did you handle commas and quotes in CSV fields?

lastHintExplanation: 'Error 400' tells a user nothing; 'That job URL doesn't look right — it should start with https://' tells them what happened and how to fix it. In CSV, a company name like 'Acme, Inc.' would split into two columns unless the field is quoted, and quotes inside a quoted field must be doubled.

STAR format for the 'hardest bug' story

title: Resume: projects that get interviews
goal: Write a one-page fresher resume with strong, specific project bullets.

concepts: One page, ATS-friendly (simple layout, no tables or text in images)
Order for freshers: summary, skills, projects, education, certifications
Bullet formula: action verb + what you built + how (tech) + result or scale
Showing proof: live links, GitHub, the demo video
Tailoring keywords to the job description without lying

build.task: Write your resume (Google Docs, Overleaf or Word, exported to PDF). Include: name, contact, LinkedIn, GitHub and portfolio links; a 2-line summary; skills grouped as Frontend, Backend, Database, Tools; projects: ApplyTrack (3–4 bullets), notes-fullstack, book-finder and the portfolio (1–2 bullets each, with live links); education. Every bullet follows action + what + how + result. Then tailor a copy for one real junior frontend or full-stack job description, matching keywords honestly. Save resume.pdf and resume-tailored.pdf in a private place, and write docs/resume-bullets.md in jobready-journey with your best 10 bullets.
acceptance: One page, plain ATS-friendly layout, exported to PDF
Projects come before education, with live and GitHub links
Every bullet starts with an action verb and names the tech
At least 3 bullets include a concrete result or number
A tailored version for one real job posting

hints: Weak: 'Made a job tracker app.' Strong: 'Built ApplyTrack, a full-stack job tracker (Angular, Express, PostgreSQL) with JWT auth, a drag-and-drop status board and a weekly analytics dashboard; 70+ automated tests, deployed with Docker on Coolify.'
Numbers that are honest for a fresher: test counts, Lighthouse scores, endpoints, pages, days to build, users who tried it.
Paste your resume into a plain-text editor. If the order and text still make sense, an ATS can read it too.
proof: Link to docs/resume-bullets.md (keep the resume itself private).

explainBack.q: Read your best ApplyTrack bullet and explain each part.

Tailoring means using the employer's words for skills you really have and putting the most relevant project first, never adding things you can't defend in an interview.

title: Capstone 1 walkthrough review
goal: Defend ApplyTrack in a mock technical interview and close Phase 5.

concepts: Project deep-dive interviews: architecture, decisions, trade-offs, scaling, what you'd change

resources.title: Tech Interview Handbook: Behavioral and project questions

build.task: Run a 45-minute mock project interview (ask a friend, a mentor, or record yourself answering): 5 minutes demo; 10 minutes architecture with your diagram; 20 minutes of questions from docs/mock-questions.md (write 15 first, e.g. 'How do you stop users seeing others' data?', 'What happens if two tabs update the same application?', 'How would you add email reminders?', 'Why PostgreSQL?', 'How would this handle 10,000 users?', 'Walk me through the status-change transaction.'); 10 minutes live code walkthrough of one feature. Record it, watch it back, and write docs/phase5-review.md: what went well, 3 answers to improve (with better versions), and what you'd change in ApplyTrack.
acceptance: 15 likely interview questions written with your answers

hints: Scaling questions don't need a complete answer: name the first bottleneck (database queries), how you'd measure it (logs, EXPLAIN ANALYZE), and one fix (indexes, pagination, caching).
For 'two tabs update the same application', talk about last-write-wins today and optimistic locking with an updated_at or version check as the improvement.
When you don't know: 'I haven't done that yet; I'd start by ... and check ...' is a strong answer.

explainBack.q: How would ApplyTrack handle two tabs editing the same application, and how could you improve it?
What would you change if you started ApplyTrack again?

lastHintExplanation: Project interviews test whether you understand what you built: why each piece exists, what breaks first under load, and what you'd improve. Saying 'currently last write wins; I'd add a version column and return 409 on mismatch' shows more maturity than pretending the system is perfect.
